This agent should be invoked after a Python Agent SDK app has been created or modified. (Tools: All tools)

- agent-sdk-dev:agent-sdk-verifier-ts: Use this agent to verify that a TypeScript Agent SDK application is properly configured, follows SDK best practices and documentation recommendations, and is ready for deployment or testing. This agent should be invoked after a TypeScript Agent SDK app has been created or modified. (Tools: All tools)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- feature-dev:code-architect: Designs feature architectures by analyzing existing codebase patterns and conventions, then providing comprehensive implementation blueprints with specific files to create/modify, component designs, data flows, and build sequences (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-explorer: Deeply analyzes existing codebase features by tracing execution paths, mapping architecture layers, understanding patterns and abstractions, and documenting dependencies to inform new development (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- plugin-dev:agent-creator: Use this agent when the user asks to "create an agent", "generate an agent", "build a new agent", "make me an agent that...", or describes agent functionality they need. Trigger when user wants to create autonomous agents for plugins. Examples:

<example>
Context: User wants to create a code review agent
user: "Create an agent that reviews code for quality issues"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to generate the agent configuration."
<commentary>
User requesting new agent creation, trigger agent-creator to generate it.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User describes needed functionality
user: "I need an agent that generates unit tests for my code"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to create a test generation agent."
<commentary>
User describes agent need, trigger agent-creator to build it.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User wants to add agent to plugin
user: "Add an agent to my plugin that validates configurations"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to generate a configuration validator agent."
<commentary>
Plugin development with agent addition, trigger agent-creator.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: Write, Read)

- plugin-dev:plugin-validator: Use this agent when the user asks to "validate my plugin", "check plugin structure", "verify plugin is correct", "validate plugin.json", "check plugin files", or mentions plugin validation. Also trigger proactively after user creates or modifies plugin components. Examples:

<example>

</example>

<commentary>

</commentary>
</example> (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>
Context: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.
Daisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"
Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.
Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"
Assistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.
Daisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"
Assistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- vercel:ai-architect: Specializes in architecting AI-powered applications on Vercel — choosing between AI SDK patterns, configuring providers, building agents, setting up durable workflows, and integrating MCP servers. Use when designing AI features, building chatbots, or creating agentic applications. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:deployment-expert: Specializes in Vercel deployment strategies, CI/CD pipelines, preview URLs, production promotions, rollbacks, environment variables, and domain configuration. Use when troubleshooting deployments, setting up CI/CD, or optimizing the deploy pipeline. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:performance-optimizer: Specializes in optimizing Vercel application performance — Core Web Vitals, rendering strategies, caching, image optimization, font loading, edge computing, and bundle size. Use when investigating slow pages, improving Lighthouse scores, or optimizing loading performance. (Tools: All tools)

- zm-implementer: Executes one step of a Zimmermann PWA Kit build plan. Use when a planned step needs to be implemented in code. Writes only the files the step names, and stops rather than expanding scope. (Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- zm-orchestrator: Scope and spec-conformance checker for an in-flight Zimmermann build. Use after an implementation step to judge whether the work delivers exactly what the plan specified — neither less nor more. Reports a verdict; never edits code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- zm-planner: Synthesises gathered evidence into an executable build plan for a Zimmermann PWA Kit story. Use after all sources have been gathered, when the findings need to become a sequenced plan with per-step pass criteria. Does not gather evidence itself and does not write code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, WebFetch)

- zm-scorer: Scores an implemented and tested Zimmermann build step and decides PASS or return-to-implementer. Use after the Tester reports. Judges quality against six axes; never edits code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- zm-tester: Tests an implemented Zimmermann build step across multiple angles and reports findings. Use after the Implementer reports a step done. Finds and reports problems; never fixes them. Dispatches its own sub-agents for parallel angles. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Agent)

import type { SystemStyleObject } from '@chakra-ui/react';
import { breakpoints } from 'app/theme/foundation';

/**
 * Recipe for the Recently Viewed Full History grid organism (SFCC-84), build plan section B1.
 * Design source: `Zimmermann_Designs` file, `3332:35655` → `Container` → `PLP Bar desktop`
 * (`3332:37131`, 1440×75, title left / item-count right) + `Sidebar` (`3332:35664`, four stacked
 * `Products Module Desktop` instances, each 1440×606, containing `Products S Desktop` cards at
 * 288×542, x = 0/384/768/1152 — a `plp`-shaped `ZimmProductCard`, not a new card; see index.tsx's
 * own `cards` JSDoc for the `variation: 'plp'` citation). **This source is provisional per
 * Marcel's 2026-09-04 precedence rule** (it is not a PDP/Recently Viewed node in the authoritative
 * `Zimmermann_Design_System_2026` file `ZimmRecentlyViewedRail`'s own recipe uses) — that ranking
 * is unaffected by the "confirmed" values below; see index.tsx's own module docblock for why both
 * things are true at once.
 *
 * Parts: `container`, `header`, `grid` — reconciled against index.tsx's own `useMultiStyleConfig`
 * reads by `ui-kits/recipeParts.test.ts`. No `card` part (contrast
 * `zimmRecentlyViewedRail.css.ts`'s own `card` part): the rail fixes a per-breakpoint PIXEL width
 * on each item because it lays out a horizontally-scrolling flex row with no requirement to fill
 * the viewport exactly. This is a real grid, not a scroller — `grid` below uses fractional
 * (`1fr`) column tracks instead, so each card's rendered width falls out of the container width
 * divided across the current column count with nothing extra to style per card; `ZimmProductCard`
 * itself still has no width/height opinion of its own (`zimmProductCard.css.ts`), same precedent
 * the rail's own docblock already establishes.
 *
 * HORIZONTAL GAP — three tiers, NOT a single uniform value (corrected 2026-09-10, closing a real
 * bug: a fuller page-node audit found the previous single 96px-everywhere value was only ever
 * confirmed for Desktop; Tablet and Mobile each have their own, different, real Figma value that
 * was never actually checked before this correction). Checked directly against the real page
 * frames' own card-group children:
 *   - Desktop (unchanged, still confirmed via the two independent sources this paragraph already
 *     cited): 96px, GENUINELY UN-TOKENISED — see `GRID_CARD_GAP_DESKTOP`'s own comment below for
 *     the full pending-token reasoning, unaffected by this correction.
 *   - Tablet (`9560:137692`, 3-card row, 834px wide): 80px, bound to a real Figma variable
 *     (`alias/space/2000`) — and unlike Desktop's 96px, this one DOES have a real registered
 *     equivalent: `--zimm-scale-5xl` (`spacing['5xl']`, `foundation/spacing.ts`), confirmed
 *     directly, no pending-token gap here.
 *   - Mobile (`9560:138463`, 2×2 grid): 40px, bound to a real Figma variable
 *     (`alias/space/gap/1000`) — also a real registered equivalent, `--zimm-scale-1000`
 *     (`spacing['3xl']`), same as this file's own `HEADER_PADDING_DESKTOP` constant below.
 * `columnGap` below is now set per-breakpoint instead of once at the base level.
 *
 * VERTICAL (ROW) GAP — 64px, and UNLIKE the horizontal gap above, this one has a real registered
 * token: `--zimm-scale-1600` (`zimmTokens.ts`), which resolves to `spacing['4xl']` —
 * independently verified directly against `foundation/spacing.ts` (`'4xl': '4rem'`, i.e. 64px),
 * not assumed from the build plan's own citation of it. Matches the real bound Figma variable
 * `section/4xl` (Designs file) / `alias/space/1600` (System file) per build plan §B1. Per this
 * step's own instruction, a REAL token is referenced directly (`var(--zimm-scale-1600)`) rather
 * than re-declared as a named constant — there is nothing to name here that isn't already named.
 *
 * COLUMN COUNT PER BREAKPOINT — three tiers: 2 (Mobile, below `breakpoints.md`), 3 (Tablet,
 * `breakpoints.md` up), 4 (Desktop, `breakpoints.xl` up).
 *   - `GRID_COLUMNS_BASE = 2` (Mobile only — matches the "2-up on the smallest breakpoint"
 *     convention `overrides/app/pages/product-list/index.tsx`'s own `SimpleGrid columns={[2, 2,
 *     4, 5]}` already establishes elsewhere in this codebase).
 *   - `GRID_COLUMNS_TABLET = 3` — originally Marcel's own direct figure (2026-09-08), not a
 *     re-derived Figma reading, since this grid's provisional design source (cited above) has no
 *     Tablet-specific node of its own. Corrected 2026-09-10: a fuller page-node audit (the same
 *     pass that fixed this file's own HORIZONTAL GAP section) checked the real Tablet page frame
 *     directly (`9560:137692`, cited above for its gap value) and found it also shows exactly 3
 *     fluid-width cards per row — the figure was already corroborated, this comment just never
 *     connected the two. Confirmed, not merely instructed, as of this correction.
 *   - `GRID_COLUMNS_DESKTOP = 4` — unchanged, the one confirmed-via-Figma value (cited above).
 *
 * HEADER HEIGHT — deliberately UNSET (contrast `zimmRecentlyViewedRail.css.ts`'s own
 * `HEADER_HEIGHT_MOBILE`/`DESKTOP`). The one Figma reading available (`3332:37131`, 75px,
 * Desktop-only) has no corroborating Mobile/Tablet reading to pair it with, and neither this
 * step's brief nor the build plan's own B1 pass criteria asks for a fixed header height at all —
 * unlike the rail, where two independent node heights (Mobile+Tablet-covering 56px, Desktop 96px)
 * were both explicitly supplied. Setting one anyway from a single, viewport-unconfirmed number
 * would be inventing a cross-viewport claim this session has no evidence for. `header` below sizes
 * itself from its own content instead (`display: flex`, vertically centred) — the same
 * "leave it simple, comment why" instruction this docblock's COLUMN COUNT section above follows
 * for the same underlying reason (one Desktop-only reading, no Tablet/Mobile counterpart).
 *
 * TITLE ROW PADDING — corrected 2026-09-10, closing a real, live-confirmed bug (Figma-vs-code
 * audit requested by Marcel, same pass that found and fixed the sibling Rail's own header padding
 * bug). The paragraph this replaces called the horizontal inset "deliberately zero... flagged for
 * confirmation" pending a real page context — that page context now exists
 * (`overrides/app/pages/recentlyViewed/index.tsx`), and checking the header row directly against
 * the three real page-composition frames (`9551:110758` Desktop, `9560:137691` Tablet,
 * `9560:138462` Mobile, same `Zimmermann_Designs` file) found the actual values are neither zero
 * nor the asymmetric split the previous revision derived from a single provisional bar node
 * (`3332:37131`) — see "Header padding" below, which replaces both the old "Header vertical
 * padding" and "Header horizontal insets" sections entirely.
 */

// Horizontal card-to-card gap, Desktop only now — see this file's own "HORIZONTAL GAP" docblock
// section above for the full per-breakpoint correction. rem, not px, matching
// zimmRecentlyViewedRail.css.ts's CARD_WIDTH_MOBILE/TABLET/DESKTOP precedent for a sizing
// (non-hairline) dimension with no foundation token yet.
const GRID_CARD_GAP_DESKTOP = '6rem'; // 96px — confirmed Figma value, checked at two independent sources (40000301:11694 "Product Card Group" master, Size=Desktop/Display=4, node 40000307:12446; and the page-level instance 3332:35655). No --zimm-scale-* equivalent (nearest neighbours: named scale 5xl=80px / 6xl=128px; numeric alias 1600=64px jumps straight to 3500=140px) — pending promotion to foundation/spacing.ts or sizes.ts by the UI designer.

// Column counts per breakpoint — see this file's own "COLUMN COUNT PER BREAKPOINT" docblock
// section above for the full reasoning and sourcing (Desktop is a confirmed Figma reading; Mobile
// and Tablet are Marcel's own direct figures, 2026-09-08, not re-derived design-asset readings).
const GRID_COLUMNS_BASE = 2; // Mobile only (below breakpoints.md) — Marcel, 2026-09-08.
const GRID_COLUMNS_TABLET = 3; // breakpoints.md up, below breakpoints.xl — Marcel, 2026-09-08.
const GRID_COLUMNS_DESKTOP = 4; // breakpoints.xl and up — confirmed (Figma nodes cited in the docblock above).

// Same Tablet/Desktop query convention (name and breakpoint) as zimmRecentlyViewedRail.css.ts's
// own identically-named constants.
const TABLET_UP_QUERY = `@media (min-width: ${breakpoints.md})`; // 768px
const DESKTOP_UP_QUERY = `@media (min-width: ${breakpoints.xl})`; // 1280px — the confirmed 4-up/288px reading itself comes from a 1440px Figma frame, inside this tier.

// Content max-width — fixed 2026-09-08, same root cause and same fix shape as
// zimmRecentlyViewedRail.css.ts's own identical bug found via live testing the same day: with no
// cap, `container`'s `width: '100%'` (and `grid`'s own, below) stretch to whatever width the page
// actually provides — confirmed via Storybook screenshot that this genuinely oversizes every card
// beyond the confirmed 288px reading, not just a cosmetic nit. 1440px is the same confirmed value
// `GRID_CARD_GAP_DESKTOP`'s own docblock derives from (4 x 288px cards + 3 x 96px gaps) — restated here as
// a width cap rather than a per-card value. Desktop-only, matching the fact that the 4-column
// layout itself only applies from this breakpoint up; neither the Mobile (2-column) nor Tablet
// (3-column) tier has a confirmed reference *width* to cap against — Marcel's own figures above
// are column counts, not card widths or a max-width reading — so both stay fluid, same "don't
// guess" reasoning as the column counts' own docblock section.
// audit-allow: derived composite (already-pending card width x confirmed column/gap counts),
// not itself a value with any promotable foundation-token equivalent.
const GRID_CONTENT_MAX_WIDTH_DESKTOP = '90rem'; // 1440px = (288px x 4 cards) + (96px x 3 gaps)

// Header padding — corrected 2026-09-10, replacing both the old "Header vertical padding" and
// "Header horizontal insets" sections (see the module docblock's own "TITLE ROW PADDING" note for
// the full correction narrative). Checked directly against the three real page-composition frames
// rather than the single provisional bar node the previous revision relied on:
//   - Desktop (`9551:110758`): 40px padding on all four sides, symmetric -- not the previous
//     asymmetric 40px-start/180px-end split, which was derived from that bar's own inner content
//     box being narrower than the frame for unrelated layout reasons, not a real padding reading.
//   - Tablet (`9560:137691`) / Mobile (`9560:138462`), identical: 32px horizontal, 20px vertical,
//     symmetric -- not the previous zero horizontal / 32px vertical (the 32px vertical value was
//     real but only for Desktop; Tablet/Mobile's own real vertical figure is smaller, 20px).
// All three real values map onto already-registered tokens: `--zimm-scale-1000` (40px),
// `--zimm-scale-800` (32px), `--zimm-scale-500` (20px, spacing['l']) -- confirmed directly against
// zimmTokens.ts, not assumed.
const HEADER_PADDING_INLINE = 'var(--zimm-scale-800)'; // 32px -- Tablet/Mobile
const HEADER_PADDING_BLOCK = 'var(--zimm-scale-500)'; // 20px -- Tablet/Mobile
const HEADER_PADDING_DESKTOP = 'var(--zimm-scale-1000)'; // 40px -- Desktop, all four sides

export const ZimmRecentlyViewedGrid = {
  parts: ['container', 'header', 'grid'],

  baseStyle: (): Record<string, SystemStyleObject> => ({
    container: {
      width: '100%',
      marginInline: 'auto',
      [DESKTOP_UP_QUERY]: {
        maxWidth: GRID_CONTENT_MAX_WIDTH_DESKTOP,
      },
    },

    header: {
      display: 'flex',
      alignItems: 'center',
      justifyContent: 'space-between',
      paddingInline: HEADER_PADDING_INLINE,
      paddingBlock: HEADER_PADDING_BLOCK,
      [DESKTOP_UP_QUERY]: {
        paddingInline: HEADER_PADDING_DESKTOP,
        paddingBlock: HEADER_PADDING_DESKTOP,
      },
    },

    grid: {
      display: 'grid',
      width: '100%',
      // `minmax(0, 1fr)`, not bare `1fr` (fixed 2026-09-10, closing a real, live-confirmed bug).
      // Bare `1fr` is shorthand for `minmax(auto, 1fr)` — a track's floor is its own content's
      // min-content size, not zero. That's invisible normally, but the size-chip row (revealed on
      // hover; see zimmProductCard.css.ts's own hoverRevealsSizeSelector block) carries a genuine,
      // non-shrinking minimum width once it enters layout (fixed-width chips, fixed `gap`, no
      // wrap) — confirmed live (Marcel, three screenshots: bug present at the narrow end of every
      // breakpoint tier — small desktop/small tablet/smaller mobile — absent at the wide end,
      // every time). At a narrow-enough column width, that minimum exceeds the column's own 1fr
      // share, so the bare-`1fr` track grows to fit it — widening every card sharing that column,
      // not just the hovered one, since a grid track's width is shared across every row. The
      // card's own image then grows too, but only as a downstream effect: `zimmProductCardMedia.
      // css.ts`'s `slide` part is `aspectRatio`-locked to its own width, so a wider column
      // mechanically produces a taller image regardless of which image (base or hover-swap) is
      // showing — confirmed directly against that file's own hover-swap implementation (both
      // images `position: absolute; inset: 0`, sized only by the aspect-ratio-locked container,
      // never by their own intrinsic size), which rules out the image swap itself as an
      // independent cause. `minmax(0, 1fr)` tells the grid the track's floor is zero instead of
      // "whatever a child needs" — the column stays at its fair share regardless of what a
      // hover-revealed child demands. Same fix family as this codebase's own existing `minWidth: 0`
      // guards on flex children (e.g. zimmProductCardContent.css.ts's `nameLink`/`priceWrapper`),
      // just expressed at the grid-track level instead.
      gridTemplateColumns: `repeat(${GRID_COLUMNS_BASE}, minmax(0, 1fr))`,
      // Per-breakpoint now — see this file's own "HORIZONTAL GAP" docblock section above for the
      // correction. Mobile/Tablet use real registered tokens directly; only Desktop's 96px is a
      // pending-token named constant.
      columnGap: 'var(--zimm-scale-1000)', // 40px — Mobile
      // Real registered token, referenced directly — see this file's own "VERTICAL (ROW) GAP"
      // docblock section above for why this one is NOT a named constant, unlike GRID_CARD_GAP_DESKTOP.
      rowGap: 'var(--zimm-scale-1600)', // 64px
      [TABLET_UP_QUERY]: {
        gridTemplateColumns: `repeat(${GRID_COLUMNS_TABLET}, minmax(0, 1fr))`,
        columnGap: 'var(--zimm-scale-5xl)', // 80px
      },
      [DESKTOP_UP_QUERY]: {
        gridTemplateColumns: `repeat(${GRID_COLUMNS_DESKTOP}, minmax(0, 1fr))`,
        columnGap: GRID_CARD_GAP_DESKTOP,
      },
    },
  }),
};
